query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: The accelerated degradation arises from a synergistic mechanism in which the multi‐phase eutectic microstructure promotes micro‐galvanic coupling at its phase boundaries and, at elevated temperature, mechanical wear continuously removes the protective oxide film that otherwise passivates the anodic phase. This wear-induced removal exposes fresh, electrochemically active surfaces (primarily on the anodic BCC phase) that, when coupled with the cathodic behavior of the FCC phase, drive localized corrosion. In turn, the corrosion at the phase boundaries weakens the structure and further exacerbates wear damage.
generation.material_initial_state: A multi‐phase eutectic high‐entropy alloy composed of at least two chemically and electrochemically distinct phases (for example, an anodic BCC phase and a cathodic FCC phase) that, under elevated temperature, develop a thin, in‐situ protective oxide film.
generation.intervention: Exposure to simultaneous mechanical abrasion (sliding wear) and a corrosive environment at elevated temperature (e.g., ~800 °C in an oxidizing atmosphere with a contaminant such as chloride ions).
generation.conditions: Testing conducted at high temperature (~800 °C) in an oxidizing environment that permits in‐situ oxide formation, with a superimposed sliding or abrasive wear load to simulate simultaneous mechanical and corrosive attack.
generation.structural_mediator: The phase boundaries between the distinct eutectic phases (e.g., between BCC and FCC regions) and the integrity of the thermally formed oxide film at these interfaces.
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperature, the alloy forms a protective oxide layer (primarily on the more cathodic FCC phase) that helps buffer corrosion. However, under sliding wear, this oxide scale is mechanically removed. The removal exposes the anodic BCC phase and sharp phase boundaries that serve as localized sites for micro‐galvanic cells. The continuous mechanical disruption coupled with these potent electrochemical gradients accelerates both wear (by reducing friction protection and structural integrity) and corrosion (by promoting anodic dissolution) in a mutually reinforcing manner.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a matched baseline subjected to only wear or only corrosion, the alloy under simultaneous wear–corrosion conditions will exhibit a total degradation rate that is significantly higher than the arithmetic sum of individual effects. Specifically, the wear depth is expected to be deeper due to recurrent oxide scale removal, and the corrosion rate of the anodic phase will be enhanced due to intensified galvanic interactions, resulting in accelerated overall mass loss.
generation.baseline: A matched sample of the same alloy subjected separately to either pure wear (in a non-corrosive inert atmosphere) or pure corrosion (static exposure without mechanical disturbance) under the same elevated temperature conditions.
generation.boundary: Elevated temperature (~800 °C), oxidizing environment containing corrosive species such as chloride ions, and applied mechanical wear (e.g., sliding or reciprocating wear) with sufficient contact force to remove oxide films.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative contribution of the wear‐induced oxide removal versus the micro‐galvanic accelerative effect is uncertain, and the magnitude of the synergistic degradation may depend on microstructural details, oxide adherence, and test parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare three sets of samples of the eutectic high-entropy alloy: one set is subjected to pure mechanical wear (using a sliding wear test) in an inert (non-corrosive) environment at 800 °C, a second set to static immersion in a corrosive medium without wear at the same temperature, and a third set to simultaneous wear and corrosion under identical temperature conditions. Measure mass loss, wear track depth, and corrosion current density, and analyze phase boundaries and oxide coverage using microscopy and surface analytical techniques.
measurements: Wear track depth and width via profilometry
Electrochemical corrosion rate (e.g., via potentiodynamic polarization)
Microstructural analysis of phase boundaries and oxide film integrity (using SEM/EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the combined wear–corrosion experiment does not exhibit a significantly higher total degradation (i.e., mass loss, wear depth, and corrosion rate) than the sum of the individual wear-only and corrosion-only tests, or if a continuous protective oxide film is found to persist uninterrupted despite wear, then the proposed synergistic mechanism involving oxide removal and micro‐galvanic coupling is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Paper card. Question: How does the molten salt corrosion behavior of the dual-phase AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy compare to conventional duplex stainless steel 2205 in a NaCl-KCl-MgCl2 environment at temperatures relevant to concentrating solar power systems?. System: AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) and duplex stainless steel 2205 (DS2205). Processing: Vacuum-arc-melting of high purity constituent elements (99.95 wt.% purity) with multiple re-melts for homogeneity; samples cut to 20 mm × 5 mm × 2 mm, polished to 1200-grit, degreased with acetone, and dried; corrosion tests performed in a custom tube furnace with 20 mm salt melt depth at 450 °C and 650 °C for 24 h. Test conditions: Molten NaCl-KCl-MgCl2 salt (45.4 wt.% MgCl2, 33 wt.% NaCl, 21.6 wt.% KCl) at 450 °C and 650 °C; immersion for 24 h; electrochemical measurements including OCP (1 h stabilization) and potentiodynamic polarization (-0.5 to 1.5 V at 1 mV/s). Findings: Corrosion rate of AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 was ~1 mm/year at 450 °C compared to ~8 mm/year for DS2205.; Corrosion rate of AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 was ~9 mm/year at 650 °C compared to ~20 mm/year for DS2205.; Mass loss for DS2205 at 650 °C was ~69 m
